# Linear stability of the elliptic relative equilibrium with $\mathbb{R}^{3}$972-gon central configurations in planar $$
M \ddot{r}=\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}
$$5-body problem 

#### Abstract

We study the linear stability of $\mathbb{R}^{3}$972-gon elliptic relative equilibrium (ERE for short), that is the Kepler homographic solution with the $\mathbb{R}^{3}$972-gon central configurations. We show that for $\mathbb{R}^{3}$976 and any eccentricity $\mathbb{R}^{3}$977, the $\mathbb{R}^{3}$972-gon ERE is stable when the central mass $N$630 is large enough. Some linear instability results are given when $N$630 is small.

From Meyer-Schmidt , there are two four-dimensional invariant symplectic subspaces, $\mathbb{R}^{3}$941 and $\mathbb{R}^{3}$947, and they are associated to the translation symmetry, dilation and rotation symmetry of the system. A symplectic matrix $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}$55 is called spectrally stable if all eigenvalues of $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}$55 belong to the unit circle $M=\operatorname{diag}\left\{m_{1}, m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}, m_{N}\right\}$009 of the complex plane. $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}$55 is called linearly stable if it is spectrally stable and semi-simple. While $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}$55 is called hyperbolic if no eigenvalues of $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}$55 are on $M=\operatorname{diag}\left\{m_{1}, m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}, m_{N}\right\}$009. The ERE is called hyperbolic (stable, resp.) if the monodromy matrix $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}$55 restricted to $M=\operatorname{diag}\left\{m_{1}, m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}, m_{N}\right\}$015, is hyperbolic (stable, resp.).

It is natural to treat $N$630 as a parameter.

There have existed many works which studied the linear stability of relative equilibria of the $\mathbb{R}^{3}$972-gon, i.e., the case with $M=\operatorname{diag}\left\{m_{1}, m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}, m_{N}\right\}$000. As far as we know, this was first started by Maxwell in his study on the stability of Saturn's rings (cf. ). Moeckel  proved that the $\mathbb{R}^{3}$972-gon is linearly stable for sufficiently large $N$630 only when $M=\operatorname{diag}\left\{m_{1}, m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}, m_{N}\right\}$062. For $M=\operatorname{diag}\left\{m_{1}, m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}, m_{N}\right\}$062, Roberts found a value $M=\operatorname{diag}\left\{m_{1}, m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}, m_{N}\right\}$064 which is proportional to $M=\operatorname{diag}\left\{m_{1}, m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}, m_{N}\right\}$065, and the $\mathbb{R}^{3}$972-gon is stable if and only if $M=\operatorname{diag}\left\{m_{1}, m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}, m_{N}\right\}$067 (cf. ). For other related works, please refer to  and reference therein.

A question proposed by Moeckel is that for a linearly stable relative equilibrium $M=\operatorname{diag}\left\{m_{1}, m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}, m_{N}\right\}$068, is there always a dominant mass, i.e., a body with a mass which is much larger than the total mass of the other bodies? Another question is whether the linearly stable relative equilibrium is always a non-degenerate minimum of the $M=\operatorname{diag}\left\{m_{1}, m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}, m_{N}\right\}$069 (cf. , Problem 15, 16).

Moeckel's conjecture is true for the relative equilibrium of $\mathbb{R}^{3}$972-gon, but we are not aware of such a result for elliptic relative equilibrium. In this paper, we study the linear stability of $\mathbb{R}^{3}$972-gon ERE. Our next main Theorems 1.1 and 1.3 show that Moeckel's conjecture is also true when $M=\operatorname{diag}\left\{m_{1}, m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}, m_{N}\right\}$072, specially Moeckel's conjecture holds for $\mathbb{R}^{3}$972-gon EREs when $\mathbb{R}^{3}$976.

# 2 The Reduction of Elliptic Relative Equilibria of $\mathbb{R}^{3}$972-gon. 

In 2005, Meyer and Schmidt used the central configuration coordinate to reduce the elliptic relative equilibria and get the essential part for the linear stability. Their central configuration coordinate is very important for us to reduce the $\mathbb{R}^{3}$972-gon ERE. For the reader's convenience, we briefly review the central configuration coordinates introduced by Meyer and Schmidt in .

# 3 The Property of the Criteria Operator 

In this section, we first introduce the stability criteria via the Morse indices in Subsection 3.1. This is based on the Maslov-type index theory described in  and the fact that the Maslov-type index is essentially the same as the Morse index for second order Hamiltonian systems. In order to estimate the Morse indices, we introduce the criteria operators with simple forms, and study their properties in Subsections 3.1, 3.2, and 3.3.

#### Abstract

We compute the fixed point index of non-degenerate central configurations for the $$
M \ddot{r}=\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}
$$5-body problem in the euclidean space of dimension $N$814, relating it to the Morse index of the gravitational potential function $\pi / 3 \mathrm{rad}$372 induced on the manifold of all maximal $\pi / 3 \mathrm{rad}$126-orbits. In order to do so, we analyze the geometry of maximal orbit type manifolds, and compute Morse indices with respect to the mass-metric bilinear form on configuration spaces. MSC Subject Class: 70F10, 55M20

# TOWARD FINITENESS OF CENTRAL CONFIGURATIONS FOR THE PLANAR SIX-BODY PROBLEM BY SYMBOLIC COMPUTATIONS 


#### Abstract

In this paper we develop symbolic computation algorithms to investigate finiteness of central configurations for the planar $$
M \ddot{r}=\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}
$$5-body problem. Our approach is based on Albouy-Kaloshin's work on finiteness of central configurations for the 5 -body problems. In their paper, bicolored graphs called $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$267-diagrams were introduced for possible scenarios when the finiteness conjecture fails, and proving finiteness amounts to exclusions of central configurations associated to these diagrams. Following their method, the amount of computations becomes enormous when there are more than five bodies. Here we introduce matrix algebra for determination of both diagrams and asymptotic orders, devise several criteria to reduce computational complexity, and verify finiteness mostly through automated deductions. For the planar six-body problem, our first algorithm effectively narrows the proof for finiteness down to 117 zw -diagrams, the second algorithm eliminates 31 of them, the last algorithm eliminates 62 other diagrams except for masses in some co-dimension 2 variety in the mass space, and leaving 24 cases unsolved.

# 1. InTRODUCTION 

The Newtonian $$
M \ddot{r}=\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}
$$5-body problem concerns $$
M \ddot{r}=\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}
$$5 mass points $N$16 moving in space in accordance with Newton's law of universal gravitation:

$r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$276

where $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$277 is the position of mass $M=\operatorname{diag}\left\{m_{1}, m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}, m_{N}\right\}$051. The position vector $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$279 $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$280 is called the configuration of the system. The system (1.1) is smooth except on the collision set $N$964 defined by

$r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$282

Configurations in $N$964 are called collision configurations.
Central configurations are non-collision configurations with the property that gravitational acceleration $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$284 of each mass point $M=\operatorname{diag}\left\{m_{1}, m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}, m_{N}\right\}$051 is a constant multiple of the vector from $N$860 to the mass center of the system. More precisely, let

$r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$287

be the mass center of the system. We say $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$288 is a central configuration for the system of masses $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$289 if there exists a positive constant $N$3, called the multiplier, such that

$r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$291

The set of central configurations is clearly invariant under similarity transformations, so two central configurations are considered equivalent if they are in the same similarity class.

Central configurations are of special importance in celestial mechanics because of their pivotal roles in self-similar solutions, singularity analysis, parabolic solutions, and bifurcations of integral manifolds. There are also practical applications such as space mission designs, asteroids' motions, modeling planetary rings, et cetera. From purely mathematical perspective, it is a profound and fascinating subject with many fundamental questions been left open. We refer readers to $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$292 for introductions and bibliographies, to $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$293 for many open questions. A fundamental question concerns the finiteness of central configurations:

Finiteness Conjecture: For any choice of $$
M \ddot{r}=\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}
$$5 positive masses, there are only finitely many similarity classes of central configurations.

The finiteness conjecture, also known as the Chazy-Wintner conjecture, has its prototype in Chazy's 1918 paper  which postulated non-degeneracy of central configurations, and phrased in present form in Wintner's classic treatise . Moulton  proved in 1910 that the collinear case $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$295 has exactly $M=\operatorname{diag}\left\{m_{1}, m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}, m_{N}\right\}$86 similarity classes of central configurations, so the finiteness conjecture is only for $N>2$201. The planar version $N>2$988 of

the finiteness conjecture was included in Smale's list of mathematical problems for the 21 st century , thereby substantially increases the attention and popularity of the topic within the mathematical community. See $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$299 for a comprehensive introduction to the history of the finiteness conjecture. In below we shall only briefly describe its current state, and progresses that are most relevant to our present work.

We consider the planar problem throughout this paper. It is well-known that the threebody problem has 5 similarity classes of central configurations , but counting central configurations for cases with more than three bodies are generally challenging tasks which involve counting real roots of sophisticated polynomial systems. Such polynomial systems vary according to variables selected, and were deduced from algebraic manipulations of (1.2), in a manner that similarity classes of central configurations are embedded into the zero locus of the polynomial system.

Hampton and Moeckel  settled the finiteness conjecture in 2006 for the four-body problem, improving an earlier work for generic mass , by using the Bernstein-KhovanskiiKushnirenko (BKK) theory in computational algebraic geometry. Their polynomial equations are primarily Albouy-Chenciner equations  and Dziobek equations . The proof involves computations of Newton polytopes for some complicated polynomials, the Minkowski sum and mixed volume, and eliminations of variables for reduced polynomial systems corresponding to faces of the Minkowski sum polytope. The number of faces is excessive, many of them correspond polynomial systems that are virtually impossible to handle manually, so the assistance of computer algebra becomes inevitable. Although computations are massive, there is no round-off error since all computations are exact and involve only integers. With similar settings and by adopting tools from tropical geometry, finiteness results were obtained for some classes of planar and spatial five-body problems by Hampton , Hampton-Jensen , Jensen-Leykin .

In 2012, Albouy and Kaloshin  settled the finiteness conjecture for the planar five-body problem except for masses in some co-dimension 2 variety in the mass space. They selected another set of variables for central configurations, yielding a different polynomial system, and devised a graph-based apparatus to tackle finiteness of real roots. When applied to the four-body problem, their approach significantly reduces the amount of computations needed for the BKK approach, and can be carried out without the assistance of computer. The case with five bodies requires much more computations, and symbolic computations were used in due course to factorize some "huge" polynomials.

The finiteness conjecture cannot be extended to arbitrary nonzero masses as a famous counterexample by Roberts  shows a continuum of central configurations for $\pi / 3 \mathrm{rad}$581 if negative masses are allowed. An interesting recent work of Yu-Zhu  based on AlbouyKaloshin's approach proves finiteness for $\pi / 3 \mathrm{rad}$312 in the presence of negative masses.

Recent advancements for the finiteness conjectures were based on insightful observations for central configurations, modern tools from computational algebraic geometry and computer algebra. If one follows previous settings and approaches directly, the case $M=\operatorname{diag}\left\{m_{1}, m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}, m_{N}\right\}$826 with general masses still seems far beyond reach due to the enormous amount of computations, and astounding complexity of polynomials involved. Finiteness for $M=\operatorname{diag}\left\{m_{1}, m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}, m_{N}\right\}$826 has been proved

for only a few exceptional cases $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$304, for some of which the exact number of central configurations were obtained.

As a step toward the finiteness conjecture for $M=\operatorname{diag}\left\{m_{1}, m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}, m_{N}\right\}$826, in this paper we follow AlbouyKaloshin's approach, introduce two families of matrices to facilitate algebraic manipulations, and design three algorithms of symbolic computations to carry out large part of computations. It is our goal to develop efficient tools to tackle the finiteness conjecture through automated deductions, save as much computing time as possible, and to leave as few unsolved cases as possible, so that further investigations can confidently depart from our remaining cases. Another aim of our work is to provide a convenient platform for this research direction via symbolic computations - by exploring more and more criteria or rules for central configurations, one can simply transform them to new subroutines and add them to our algorithms. For this purpose we open our source codes with Mathematica in Appendices, where we also include clear instructions on correspondence between subroutines and criteria been applied.

In  bicolored graphs called $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$267-diagrams were introduced for possible scenarios when the finiteness conjecture fails, and proving finiteness amounts to exclusions of central configurations associated to these diagrams. In their paper, proving finiteness for the case $\pi / 3 \mathrm{rad}$312 was narrowed down to $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$308-diagrams, the case $\pi / 3 \mathrm{rad}$581 to $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$310-diagrams. Comparing with other works about finiteness, their settings appear to be most ideal for the case $M=\operatorname{diag}\left\{m_{1}, m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}, m_{N}\right\}$826, although we have not resolve all cases. Here we introduce matrix algebra for determination of both $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$267-diagrams and asymptotic orders of primary variables, devise several criteria to reduce computational complexity, and use our algorithms to verify finiteness. Our first algorithm narrows down the case $M=\operatorname{diag}\left\{m_{1}, m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}, m_{N}\right\}$826 to $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$314-diagrams, the second algorithm eliminates 31 of them, and the third algorithm finds mass relations for 62 diagrams, one of which is impossible for positive masses. This leaves finiteness of 24 cases unsolved.

The paper is organized as follows. We will begin with a brief introduction of AlbouyKaloshin's approach in section 2. In particular, we recall their concepts of singular sequences, $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$267-diagrams, coloring rules, and some estimates that are critical to our analysis and algorithms. In Section 3 we associate $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$267-diagrams to their adjacency matrices, and establish several matrix rules. Some matrix rules are direct consequence of coloring rules, some are more sophisticated. In section 4, we associate $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$267-diagrams another set of matrices, called order matrices, which tracks possible orders of primary variables. Several criteria for order matrices will be proved. Section 5 shows the procedure of collecting polynomial equations. Then, in section 6 , we provide an effective algorithm to generate all possible $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$267-diagrams. The algorithm for generating order matrices will be given in section 7. Based on these order matrices, we either eliminate the $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$267-diagram directly or collect polynomial equations for the diagram. Section 8 shows an algorithm for eliminations and generating mass relations. Sections 9, 10 are respectively applications of our algorithms to the fourand five-body problems. Section 11 contains the major progress of our work, namely the application to the six-body problem. Appendices contain source codes of our Mathematica programs and details of some frequently appeared mass relations.

# 2. Singular SEQUENCES, $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$267-DIAGRAMS, AND COLORING RULES 

This section is a brief introduction of Albouy and Kaloshin's method  for planar central configurations. We introduce their formulations for normalized central configurations, the concept of singular sequences, $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$267-diagrams, and then summarize most of their estimates and coloring rules. These concepts and rules are necessary preliminaries for our arguments and algorithms in subsequent sections.

For a singular sequence, we write down indices of bodies, draw a circle around index $N$075 if $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$398 has the maximum order (i.e. $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$411 ), and draw a stroke between $N$075 and $N$279 if $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$414. 2.5. Order estimates and coloring rules. Here we summarize some key estimates and coloring rules in .

Theorem 2.4 (One Color Rules). In the z-diagram of a singular sequence, we have the following properties.
(Rule 1a) These exists at least one z-stroke. At each end of a z-stroke, there is either another z-stroke emanating from it or a z-circle around it. At each z-circle, there is a z-stroke emanating from it.
(Rule 1b) If bodies $N$075 and $N$279 are z-close, then they are both z-circled or both not z-circled.
(Rule 1c) In an isolated component, the center of mass of bodies in this component is $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$42-close to the origin.
(Rule 1d) In an isolated component of the z-diagram, if there is a z-circle, there is another one. Moreover, these z-circles can't be all z-close together.
(Rule 1e) In an isolated component, there is a maximal z-stroke if and only if there is a $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$42-circle.
Rules 1a-1e hold if "z-" are replaced by " $N$067-".
Theorem 2.5 (Two Colors Rules). In the zw-diagram of a singular sequence, we have the following properties.
(Circling Method) If there is a w-stroke (resp. z-stroke) between $N$075 and $N$279, then $N$075 and $N$279 are both z-circled (resp. w-circled) or both not z-circled (resp. w-circled).
(Rule 2a) For each zw-edge in the diagram, there is another z-stroke and w-stroke emanating from it.
(Rule 2b) If there are two consecutive zw-edges, there is a third zw-edge such that these three edges form a triangle.
(Rule 2c) Consider two consecutive edges which are not part of a triangle. Suppose they are an edge between 1,2 and an edge between 2,3. Then the cluster schemes are $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$492 or $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$493. In this situation, we say there is skew clustering.
(Cor. of Rule 2c) If there are two consecutive z-edges ( $N$067-edges) which are not part of a triangle in the zw-diagram, they can not be both maximal.

(Rule 2d) Consider a cycle of edges, the list of z-separations in this cycle, and the maximal order within the list. At least two of these z-separations are of this order, and the corresponding edges are of the same type. Moreover, if there are exactly two zseparations of this order, then the two z-separations are equivalent (i.e. $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$495 if these edges are between $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$496 and between $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$497 ). Same rule holds if " $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$42-" are replaced by " $N$067-".
(Rule 2e) If three edges form a triangle, then they are of the same type, the corresponding $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$42-separations are of the same order, and the corresponding $N$067-separations are of the same order.
(Cor. of Rule 2e) Consider any three vertices, the number of strokes joining them is $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$502, or 6 .
(Rule 2f) Consider a triangle with vertices $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$503 formed by edges in the diagram. Suppose there exists $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$504 and other vertices $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$505 such that for each $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$506 $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$507, there are at least two edges connecting $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$508 with vertices in $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$509. Then there is an edge between any two of $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$510, these edges are of the same type, their corresponding z-separations are of the same order, their corresponding $N$067 separations are of the same order.
(Rule 2g) If there are four edges forming a quadrilateral, then the opposite edges have the same type.
(Rule 2h) If there are bodies $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$512 such that $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$513 for all $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$514 and $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$515, then there is another pair of bodies $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$496 such that $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$517.
(Cor. of Rule 2h) If there is a zw-edge in the diagram, then there is another one.
Some other propositions from [4, Prop. 1,2,4] for singular sequences are also helpful for our purpose:

$$5, then $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$522 and the origin form a cluster of size $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$523; i.e. $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$524.

Proposition 2.7. If there is some $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$525 such that $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$526 for all $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$527, then there are some $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$528 such that $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$529 and $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$530.

Proposition 2.8. Suppose the diagram has exactly one maximal z-edge, and it forms an isolated component, say bodies 1 and 2 are endpoints of this edge. If $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$531, then there is no $N$075 with $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$533 such that $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$534 for all $N$279 satisfying $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$536 and $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$537.

These propositions hold if " $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$42 " and " $N$067 " were switched.
2.6. Remarks on proof for finiteness. In the case of 4 bodies, Albouy and Kaloshin first use coloring rules to construct all possible diagrams associated to singular sequences. For some of those diagrams, they find an algebraic relation for masses that a singular sequence associated to the diagram necessarily satisfies. There are four diagrams with simple mass relations and a diagram that does not yield any mass relation.

In the proof for finiteness, they often use the following arguments:

- If there are infinitely many normalized central configurations, then there is some polynomial function $\pi / 3 \mathrm{rad}$993 taking infinitely many values, and there is a singular sequence over which $\pi / 3 \mathrm{rad}$993 tends to 0 or $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$542.
- A singular sequence over which $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$543 (or $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$542 ) is impossible in some diagrams, therefore another specified polynomial $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$545 tends to 0 (or $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$542 ) over this singular sequence.
- Over a singular sequence, a polynomial $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$547 (or $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$542 ) implies that there is another singular sequence over which $\pi / 3 \mathrm{rad}$993 tends to $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$542 (or 0 ).
- A singular sequence over which $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$547 (or $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$542 ) is impossible in some diagrams, therefore the masses must satisfy the mass relation of one of other diagrams.

Roughly speaking, the idea of proof for finiteness is to take several singular sequences from the set of normalized central configurations, they are associated to different diagrams, but there are no masses satisfying all of these corresponding mass relations.

# 3. Matrix rules for Singular Sequences 

In this section we define $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$42-matrix, $N$067-matrix, and $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$267-matrix associate to a singular sequence of central configurations, and establish algebraic rules for these matrices. Most of these matrix rules are deduced from estimates, coloring rules, and propositions in the previous section. Some of them are immediate corollaries of coloring rules, but some others are more sophisticated. They provide effective tools for the implementation of our algorithms.

Definition 3.1. Given a singular sequence of central configurations for the $$
M \ddot{r}=\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}
$$5-body problem and consider the corresponding $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$267-diagram. The adjacency matrix for its $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$42-diagram with $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$42-circles regarded as self-loops is called the $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$42-matrix associated to the singular sequence. More precisely, the $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$42-matrix is the symmetric $N$434 binary matrix $N$954 given by

$r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$564

Similarly, the $N$067-matrix associated to the singular sequence is the adjacency matrix for the $N$067-diagram with $N$067-circles regarded as self-loops. It is the $N$434 binary matrix $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$569 given by

$r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$570

The $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$267-matrix of the singular sequence is the $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$572 binary matrix $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$573. We say $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}$25 and $M=\operatorname{diag}\left\{m_{1}, m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}, m_{N}\right\}$23 are companion matrices of each other.

Definition 3.2. A connected component of a $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$42-matrix $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}$25 (resp. $N$067-matrix $M=\operatorname{diag}\left\{m_{1}, m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}, m_{N}\right\}$23 ) is a subset $\mathbb{R}^{3}$38 of $\pi / 3 \mathrm{rad}$213 such that the principal submatrix obtained by removing all $\pi / 3 \mathrm{rad}$110-th columns and all $\pi / 3 \mathrm{rad}$110-th rows with $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$584 from $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$585 (resp. $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$586 ) is a maximal principal submatrix whose entries are all positive.

Definition 3.3. A $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$42-matrix $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}$25 (resp. $N$067-matrix $M=\operatorname{diag}\left\{m_{1}, m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}, m_{N}\right\}$23 ) is said to be fully connected if $\pi / 3 \mathrm{rad}$213 is a connected component of $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}$25 (resp. $M=\operatorname{diag}\left\{m_{1}, m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}, m_{N}\right\}$23 ).

Our matrix rules are necessary conditions for possible $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$42-matrices and $N$067-matrices. They can be classified according to types of diagrams involved. If a rule concerns either the $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$42-diagram or the $N$067-diagram, but not both, we say it is a monocolored matrix rule. If the criterion concerns the $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$267-diagram, we call it a bicolored matrix rule. It is worth noting that monocolored matrix rules are not merely matrix formulations of one color rules, neither are bicolored matrix rules simply corollaries of two color rules.

In below, we will classify matrix rules according basic features of matrices, and the number of vertices involved. Table 1 shows our classification and their correspondence with coloring rules. One of them does not come from any coloring rule. Many of them require estimates and propositions in the previous section but we omit these dependence in the table.

Names of our matrix rules are mostly intuitive. For example, rules about trace are restrictions on traces of $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$42-, $N$067-, or $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$267-matrices, or restrictions to cases with a fixed trace; rules about triangles are restrictions on three vertices in the diagram; rules about quadrilaterals

are restrictions on four vertices, and so on. An exception is the rule about a single edge, we name it the Rule of Circling because it is an immediate consequence of the Circling Method.

Proof. Part (a) follows immediately from Rule 1d.

Assume hypothesis of (c). implies $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$700, for otherwise it would contradict the Corollary of Rule 2c (if there is no edge between $N$043 and $\pi / 3 \mathrm{rad}$110 ) or Rule $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$703 (if there is a $N$067-edge between $N$043 and $\pi / 3 \mathrm{rad}$110 ).

# 4. ORDER MATRICES FOR SINGULAR SEQUENCES 

In $$

In this section we introduce order matrices to discuss orders for three sets of variables, also in terms of power functions of $N$855. These three sets of variables are "positions" $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$398 's, $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$400 's, "separations" $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$351 's, $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$352 's, and "distances" $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$350 's.

4.1. Levels of orders and order matrices. Recall that a sequence $N>2$006 of non-zero complex numbers satisfies $$

M \ddot{r}=\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}

Let us extend this concept a bit further. Given a sequence $\pi / 3 \mathrm{rad}$969 of complex numbers, possibly with infinitely many zeros, we say $\pi / 3 \mathrm{rad}$969 has order strictly less than $$

While Estimate 1 provides bounds for orders of separations and distances, separations and distances may not have well-defined orders in terms of power functions of $N$855, neither are position variables. But it makes sense to say a variable's order is strictly between some $$
M \ddot{r}=\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}

In order to simplify discussions and clear the way for symbolic computations, we discretize the problem by dividing possible orders into a few levels, and then introduce order matrices to record possible levels of these variables.

Based on Estimates 1 and 2, we divide orders of positions and separations into six levels:
Level 0 : the order is strictly less than $$

Since separations satisfy $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$466, level 0 is only possible for positions.
Distances satisfy $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$465, so we divide their orders differently:
Level 1: the order is $N$855
Level 2: the order is strictly between $N$855 and 1
Level 3: the order is 1

Level 5: the order is $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$964

As soon as ranges of levels for positions and separations were determined, our next goal is to find a "suitable" collection of $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$267-order matrices which covers $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$267-orders of the singular sequence. They will automatically generate a collection of $N$892-order matrices which covers $N$892-orders of the singular sequence. Loosely speaking, a "suitable" collection of $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$267-order matrices are expected to meet two criteria:
(i) The collection is not too big for the purpose of symbolic computations.
(ii) Members of the collection yield polynomial equations which are useful in generating mass relations for the singular sequence.
These two criteria compete with each other. If orders of positions and separations are more precise, we are more likely to obtain useful polynomial equations from them, but this comes at the price of having larger collection of $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$267-order matrices. We will illustrate this point by showing a simple example. This example also provides some incentives for our methods of choosing the collection $N$795.

Comparing with the BKK approach in , this procedure is in essence the same as taking one face of the Minkowski sum polytope and considering its corresponding reduced system. This section shows some details of how such polynomial equations are to be collected.

In the process of picking out leading order terms for $$

# 6. Algorithm I - Determine $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$267-diagrams 

Our program contains three algorithms: the first one is to find possible diagrams; the second one is to search for possible orders of various variables associated to a diagram; the last one is to find mass relations for diagrams. All of them use symbolic computations, thus all outputs are exact and free from round-off errors.

This section is devoted to the first algorithm. The following is the outline of the algorithm. See Appendix I for codes with Mathematica.
(I.1) Initial selection of possible $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$42-matrices
(a) Sort symmetric binary matrices according to column sums and diagonals

(b) Eliminate matrices with trace 1
(c) Classify them according to trace
(I.2) Apply monocolored matrix rules
(a) Rule of Column Sums
(b) First Rule of Trace-2 Matrices
(c) Second Rule of Triangles
(d) First Rule of Quadrilaterals
(e) First Rule of Triangles
(f) Rule of Trace-3 Matrices
(g) Rule of Trace-0 Principal Minors
(I.3) Produce possible $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$267-matrices
(a) Produce possible $N$067-matrices
(b) Classify $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$42-matrices according to connectedness
(c) Match $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$42 - and $N$067-matrices based on Rule of Fully Connected Companions
(I.4) Apply bicolored matrix rules
(a) Rule of Circling
(b) Second Rule of Trace-2 Matrices
(c) Third Rule of Triangles
(d) Rule of Two Column Sums
(e) Fourth Rule of Triangles
(f) Rule of Connected Components
(g) Second Rule of Quadrilaterals
(h) Rule of Pentagons
(I.5) Generate $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$267-diagrams associated to remaining $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$267-matrices

The whole procedure involves large amount of computations. Elimination of $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$267-matrices by brute force may result in crashes of the computer program when $$
M \ddot{r}=\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}
$$698, so effectively reducing the amount of computations is a critical part of our program. In below we discuss some details of the program, except the easy step (I.5).

Step (I.1). In the initial selection of possible $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$42-matrices, by the First Rule of Trace, we don't produce matrices with trace 1. To delete some equivalent cases at the beginning, without loss of generality we may assume $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$42-circled bodies have larger indices; that is, we may assume $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$42-matrices satisfy the following condition:

$$
M \ddot{r}=\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}
$$820

The number of such $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$42-matrices is $$
M \ddot{r}=\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}
$$822. We divide these matrices according to their traces into $$

$$5 classes $$

# 8. Algorithm III - Eliminations and mass relations 

For each $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$267-matrix $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$573, we collect a system of polynomial equations as outlined in section 5 . This system of polynomial equations are necessary conditions for the existence of singular sequence associated to $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$573. Our hope is to apply elimination theory to obtain polynomial equations with only mass variables, we call these equations mass relations associated to $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$573. By doing so, we conclude that masses outside the zero loci of these mass relations cannot possibly result in a singular sequence associated to $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$573. If we are able to do the same for every $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$267-matrix, then we conclude finiteness of central configurations for masses outside the zero loci of a family of mass relations. Since central configurations are invariant by scaling masses, such zero loci should be a co-dimension 2 algebraic variety in the mass space.

Given $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$267-matrix $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$573. For the four-body problem, we obtain five diagrams for singular sequences in Figure 1 by Algorithm I. These diagrams and mass relations obtained from Algorithms II, III are the same as those in , except the appearance of some additional factors for the third diagram. This is no coincidence since our algorithms were designed to embody their ideas in a mechanical process. This section demonstrates applications of our algorithms to these diagrams. Similar cases appear multiple times for $N$797.

In fact, as shown in $N$0189, finiteness can be achieved without appealing to any mass relation for this particular diagram. The idea is to introduce a dominant polynomial in distances which is bounded on singular sequences approaching this particular diagram. Using a basic property of dominant polynomials, it ensures the existence of a singular subsequence approaching one of the other four diagrams. Therefore, to conclude finiteness, it is sufficient to exclude the other four diagrams.

# 11. THE CASE $M=\operatorname{diag}\left\{m_{1}, m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}, m_{N}\right\}$826 

Our main result for the six-body problem is
Theorem 11.1. There are at most 85 possible zw-diagrams for the planar six-body problem. Among them, at least 61 of them are impossible except for positive masses in a co-dimensional 2 variety of the mass space.

Indeed, we obtained 117 zw -diagrams by Algorithm I. See Figures 3, 4, 5, 6. Among them, there are 27 diagrams that were eliminated by Algorithm II directly:

$N$0567

and diagrams $N$0568 were eliminated by Algorithm II indirectly. Another diagram, NO. 116, can be eliminated by Algorithm III. See $N$0569 below.

We will demonstrate how our algorithms eliminates diagrams $N$0568 and generate mass relations for NO. 116 and 61 other diagrams, and that leaves 24 diagrams unsolved. Ideally, the finiteness conjecture can be tackled by the arguments in $N$0571; namely, to

find a dominant polynomial that stays bounded for singular sequences approaching all of the 24 remaining diagrams. We do not know whether such a dominant polynomial exists. A more practical approach is probably to rule out some of them on a case-by-case basis, then find a suitable dominant polynomial afterwards. We have not finish this task, thereby leaving an incomplete puzzle for future investigations.

# Appendix I: Program for Algorithm I by Mathematica 

After compiling the program, use function "zwmatrices" and input the number of bodies to find out $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$267-matrices. To monitor performance, one can easily output the number of $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$267-matrices remaining and cumulative time used after each subroutine. We remove these parts for brevity. Some remarks were added using " $N$1304 " for clarifications.

```
zwmatrices[nn_]:=(
n = nn;pm = Permutations@Table[k,{k,n}];
ConnectedMatrixQ[x_]:=
    Count[Flatten[IdentityMatrix + Sum[MatrixPower[x,k],{k,1,n-1}]],0] ==0;
zpart[{z.,w.}]:=z;wpart[{z.,w.}]:=w;
trianglepart[x_]:=Table[If[i\left[\nabla f\left(\mathbf{x}^{(k)}\right)\right]2 j,x[[i,j]],0],{i,1,n},{j,1,n}];
(* BEGIN SELECTION OF z-MATRICES *)
(* Collect all symmetric binary matrices, sort them according to column
    sums and diagonals, then delete duplicates *)
mxsort[x..?ArrayQ]:=x[[\#\#]]&@@(Ordering[x ~ Total ~ {#}]&/@{1,1});
mxreorder[x..?ArrayQ]:=x[[\#\#]]&@@(Ordering[Diagonal]&/@{1,1});
A = Tuples[{0,1},n(n-1)/2];a = Table[k(k-1)/2,{k,1,n+1}];
S = {0} ~ Join ~ Table[k,{k,2,n}];
V = Array[If [#1 > #2,0,1]&,{n+1,n}];
F[x_]:=Array[If [#1 \#2, x[[ a[[n-Abs[#1 - #2] ]] + Min[#1, #2]]],0]&,{n,n}];
fmx0 = Table[F[A[]], {k,1,Length}];
fmx = Table[Table[DiagonalMatrix[V[[n-j+1]]] + fmx0[], {k,1,Length[fmx0]}],{j, S}];
Do[fmxs = Table[mxsort@fmx[][], {k,1,Length[fmx[]]}];
fmx[] = DeleteDuplicates, {j,1,n}];
Do[fmx[] = Table[mxreorder@fmx[][], {k,1,Length[fmx[]]}],{j,1,n}];
Do[fmx[] = DeleteDuplicates[fmx[]], {j,1,n}];
(* Rule of Column Sums *)
RuleCSQ[x_]:=Count[Total@x,1] == 0&&Count[Total@x,0] <n;
Do[fmx[] = Select[fmx[], RuleCSQ], {k,1,n}];
(* First Rule of Trace-2 Matrices *)
RuleTr2Part1Q[x_]:=x[[n,n-1]]==1;
fmx[] = Select[fmx[], RuleTr2Part1Q];
twolinesSP[x_]:=Flatten[Table[(x[[i,n]]+x[[i,n-1]]+x[[n-1,n]]),{i,1,n-2}]]];
RuleTr2MxPart2Q[x_]:=(Count[twolinesSP,2] ==0);
fmx[] = Select[fmx[], RuleTr2MxPart2Q];
(* Second Rule of Triangles *)
prtriangle3[x_]:=Flatten[Table[
    $N$1305 2];
RuleTriangle2Q[x_]:=Count[prtriangle3@x,3] == 0;
```

$$5 ] or FindOrder $N$1561 to generate the optimal $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$267-order matrices of Type 1 and the collections $N$0038 for diagram $$
M \ddot{r}=\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}
$$5. A default time constraint is set to prevent from enumerating all Type 2 or Type $$
M \ddot{r}=\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}
$$968-order matrices when there are too many possibilities. The optional argument $N$627 is to change this time constraint.

The optimal $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$267-order matrices of Type 1 is denoted $N$1568, and the collection $$

# CLASSIFICATION OF STACKED CENTRAL CONFIGURATIONS IN $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$30 

#### Abstract

We classify the extensions of $$
M \ddot{r}=\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}
$$5-body central configurations to $(n+1)$-body central configurations in $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$30, in both the collinear case and the non-collinear case. We completely solve the two open questions posed by Hampton. This classification is related with study on co-circular and co-spherical central configurations. We also obtain a general property of co-circular central configurations.

## 1. InTRODUCTION

Central configurations are important in the classical N-body problems. They naturally arise in the study of the self-similar solutions, and they are involved in the classification of the topology of integral manifolds . In the collection of important open problems in celestial mechanics compiled by Albouy-Cabral-Santos , half of the list is on central configurations. Readers are referred to $$N$2529(n+k)$-body central configurations extended from $$
M \ddot{r}=\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}
$$5-body central configurations by adding $N$075 bodies are called stacked central configurations. For instance, the Lagrangian equilateral triangle central configuration is a stacked central configuration. It is also well-known that a pyramidal central configuration can be obtained by adding one mass to a co-circular central configuration . Hampton introduced stacked central configurations in 2005 . Many other examples of stacked central configurations were constructed, see .

Hampton also raises two questions regarding stacked central configuration $:$
(1) In addition to symmetric collinear configurations $\mathbb{R}^{3}$21, the square or a regular tetrahedron with a mass at its center and the square pyramidal configuration are there any five-body central configurations with a subset forming a four-body central configuration?
(2) Are there any five-body non-collinear central configurations all of whose four-body subsets form a central configuration?
There are some works devoted to this two questions. Assuming that a five-body central configuration is co-planar and non-collinear, in 2013, Fernandes-Mello  and Alvarez Ramírez-Santos-Vidal  announced independently that such configuration must be a square with equal masses and one mass at the center of the square. Though the paper  contains several inspirational observations, some argument is problematic. In 2018, Fernandes-Mello  fix the proof, see Remark 6. However, the two questions remain open.

In this work, we classify the ways by which an $$
M \ddot{r}=\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}
$$5-body $(n \geq 2)$N$2536(n+1)$-body central configuration in $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$30. With this classification, we solve the two open questions completely. We also find one general property of co-circular central configurations. It plays a crucial role in our study of the extensions of co-circular central configurations.

There are two cases. Firstly, the extended $(n+1)$-body central configuration is collinear. In this case, we show that extensions happen only for $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}$784. So the question of collinear extensions has already been answered by Euler . Secondly, the extended $(n+1)$-body central configuration is non-collinear. In this case, it has been proved by Fernandes-Mello  that it is necessary that the $$
M \ddot{r}=\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}
$$5-body central configuration lies on a common circle or sphere. Our approach is different from theirs. Our results contain not only the necessary conditions, but sufficient conditions as well. Thus, we can classify all the extensions.

Let $N$892 be the radius of the circle (sphere) and $r_{0}=\left(\right40\right)^{\right42}$, the cubic root of the ratio of total mass $N$630 and the multiplier $N$3 of the $$
M \ddot{r}=\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}
$$5-body configuration. The co-circular (co-spherical) central configurations can extend if their mass center equals their geometric center. They can also extend if $r_{0} \geq r$N$2548r_{0}=r$ for the co-spherical case.

Thus, the measurement of $N$892 and $r_{0}$N$2551r_{0}>r$ holds for all four, five, and six-body co-circular central configurations. Together with the works of Hampton  and Cors-Roberts  on the co-circular fourbody problem, we find all the extensions of four-body central configurations to five-body central configurations. And we answer Hampton's two questions completely.

The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we state the main results. In Section 3, we prove the main results. In Section 4, we discuss the extensions of two, three, four, and five-body central configurations. In Section 5, we find several examples of co-spherical central configurations whose mass center equals the geometric center.

Proposition 1. In $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$30, there are only three types of $(n+1)$-body central configurations all of whose $$

These central configurations are called co-circular central configurations, in the planar case and co-spherical central configurations, in the spatial case. Theorem 6. There are only three types of five-body central configurations of which a four-body sub configuration is central:

- the square with equal masses and an arbitrary mass $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}$750 at the center;

# ON THE SECTIONAL CURVATURE ALONG CENTRAL CONFIGURATIONS 


#### Abstract

In this paper we characterize planar central configurations in terms of a sectional curvature value of the Jacobi-Maupertuis metric. This characterization works for the $N$-body problem with general masses and any $1 / r^{\mathbf{x}96}$ potential with $\pi / 3 \mathrm{rad}$100. We also obtain dynamical consequences of these curvature values for relative equilibrium solutions. These curvature methods work well for strong forces $(\mathbf{x}96 \geq 2)$.


## 1. InTRODUCTION

Since Euler and Lagrange, central configurations form a main theme in studies of the $N$-body problem. Such configurations are characterized by the property that upon dropping the bodies from rest, they homothetically shrink to a total collision. Those of the 3-body problem have long been well known. They are exactly equilateral triangles due to Lagrange and certain collinear configurations found by Euler.

Every central configuration leads to homographic solutions of the $N$-body problem: ones whose configuration evolves only by rotation or scaling. Such solutions are the only explicit solutions known for the $N>2$ body problems. See the nice references $$ for more on central configurations.

By the planar $N$-body problem with a $1 / r^{\mathbf{x}96}$ potential, we mean the movement of $N$ point masses $q_{1}, \right47, q_{N} \nabla08 \left[\nabla f\left(\mathbf{x}^{(k)}\right)\right]162$N$3025
m_{k} \left[\nabla f\left(\mathbf{x}^{(k)}\right)\right]163_{k}=\left[\nabla f\left(\mathbf{x}^{(k)}\right)\right]164}
$N$3026
U:=\frac{1}{\mathbf{x}96} \right65_{i<j} \right83 m_{j}}{\left|q_{i}-q_{j}\right|^{\mathbf{x}96}}
$N$30271 / r^{\mathbf{x}96}$ potential $\mathbb{R}^{3}$21 and $m_{k}>0$ are the masses. A central configuration is a configuration $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$279 $\left(q_{1}, \right47, q_{N}\right)$N$2641\nabla U(q)=\geq22 q$ for some $r=\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}\right), r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$46.

Here we will study these central configurations using the Jacobi-Maupertuis principle. This principle reparametrizes solutions of a natural mechanical system at a fixed energy level as geodesics of a certain metric (eq. (6) below), which we call the JM-metric for short.

It is well known that the sectional curvature values of a Riemannian metric at a point determine the local behavior of nearby geodesics, governing the convergence or divergence of neighboring geodesics passing through this point. Namely, negative values imply nearby geodesics diverge more than those in a Euclidean plane, while positive values imply they diverge less (see Figure 1). These comparisons are made by examining growths of Jacobi Fields, which in turn are used to express the linearization of the geodesic flow, see for instance $$. In this paper we examine some sectional curvatures of the JM-metric at central configurations.

Later, M. Barbosu and B. Elmabsout in  also computed some sectional curvatures along this Lagrange solution with equal masses, observing that certain energy values lead to negative sectional curvatures over this solution and noting that this negative curvature leads to 'instability' of these solutions. More precisely, negative sectional curvatures over a suitable set of planes along the orbit leads to exponential growth of certain Jacobi fields in forwards or backwards time. Consequently the linearized Poincaré return map of the geodesic flow may have eigenvalues off of the unit circle. This instability is called spectral instability:

Definition 1. A periodic orbit is spectrally unstable if its linearized first return map has an eigenvalue $N$3 with $|\geq22| \left[\nabla f\left(\mathbf{x}^{(k)}\right)\right]9 1$.

There is also the weaker notion of linear instability:
Definition 2. A periodic orbit is linearly unstable if its linearized first return map is not diagonalizable or it is spectrally unstable.

Since reparametrizing orbits has no effect on the Poincaré first return map, computations using the geodesic flow of the JM-metric will lead to the same eigenvalues as those associated to the flow

of the original equations of motion on a fixed energy level. The reference  allows a computation of the sectional curvatures through complex planes (Proposition 1 below), from which we obtain the following Barbosu-Elmabsout inspired result:

Theorem 1. When $\mathbf{x}96>2$, the 'waist' is the relative equilibrium solution. The boundaries correspond to collision or escape to infinity.

Conjecture 1. Consider the planar $N$-body problem under a $1 / r^{\mathbf{x}96}$N$3067m_{k}>0$N$26460<\mathbf{x}96<2$. Let $\mathbb{R}^{3}$49 be a central configuration.

Then at least one of the two classes of periodic homographic motions, $z(t) q$, are spectrally unstable:
(i) those near the circular relative equilibrium solution,
(ii) those near the homothetic 'total collapse' solution.

Remark 2. Investigating stability properties of homographic solutions has been well studied, (see e.g. : problem 15). In particular the Lagrange configuration when $\pi / 3 \mathrm{rad}$573 by perturbation and numerical methods (see $$N$3073$ for other recent applications of Maslov-type index theory).

It can be shown (see remark 4) that for any given central configuration $\mathbb{R}^{3}$49, there is either a family of planes with negative sectional curvature tangent to the relative equilibrium solution through $\mathbb{R}^{3}$49 or a family of planes with mostly negative sectional curvatures tangent to the homothetic total collapse solution through $\mathbb{R}^{3}$49. This motivated the conjecture, since we expect the negative curvatures over these planes to give growth of Jacobi fields and instability. However, it remains to be seen whether the family of planes lies tangent to a family of geodesics i.e. whether there are Jacobi fields staying close to the family of planes for one period of the motion.

For comparison, figure 3 (established by Martinez et. al ) shows detailed stability properties of the Lagrange solution for the classical $\pi / 3 \mathrm{rad}$573 force law, and fits with our conjecture.

# CENTRAL CONFIGURATIONS WITH DIHEDRAL SYMMETRY 

#### Abstract

As an application of the representation theory for the dihedral groups, we study the symmetric central configurations in the $$
M \ddot{r}=\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}
$$5-body problem where $$
M \ddot{r}=\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}
$$5 equal masses are placed at the vertices of a regular $$
M \ddot{r}=\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}
$$5-gon. Since the Hessian matrices at these configurations are typically very large, particularly when $$
M \ddot{r}=\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}
$$5 is large, computations of their eigenvalues present a challenging problem. However, by decomposing the action of the dihedral groups into irreducible representations, we show that the Hessians can be simplified to a block-diagonal matrix with small blocks, of the sizes at most $M=\operatorname{diag}\left\{m_{1}, m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}, m_{N}\right\}$591. This is due to fact that the action of a dihedral group can be represented as a block-diagonal matrix with small irreducible blocks. In the end, the eigenvalues can be explicitly obtained by simply computing eigenvalues of these small block matrices.

M \ddot{r}=\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}
$$5 particles such that the relative distance of the particles can be maintained throughout a particular solution. It turns out that the central configurations are critical points of the function $\left[\nabla f\left(\mathbf{x}^{(k)}\right)\right]799 U$N$3488

$$

A notable central configuration is where the $$
M \ddot{r}=\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}
$$5 equal masses are positioned at the vertices of a regular $$
M \ddot{r}=\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}
$$5-gon. This configuration exhibits inherent symmetries that offer avenues for simplification and deeper understanding. As it is a critical point for the function $\left[\nabla f\left(\mathbf{x}^{(k)}\right)\right]799 U$, it is crucial to investigate the eigenvalues of the Hessian to uncover additional properties of the solution.

For the Newtonian $$
M \ddot{r}=\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}
$$5-body problem, for each planar central configuration $z_{0} \nabla08 \left[\nabla f\left(\mathbf{x}^{(k)}\right)\right]825^{2 n}$, there is correspondingly a class of periodic solutions where $$
M \ddot{r}=\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}
$$5 particles move in concentric circles, keeping their relative positions fixed. These solutions are called relative equilibria. A relative equilibria is degenerate if the Hessian for the corresponding central configuration has a non-trivial nullspace. In 1976, Palmore studied the degeneracies of relative equilibria for the $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}$801-body problem, calculating eigenvalues by decomposing the tangent space into invariant subspaces. Through this approach, Palmore identified a critical mass value $m^{*}$ at which the relative equilibria degenerate. Building upon this work, Moeckel explored the linear stability of such symmetric configurations in the $$
M \ddot{r}=\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}
$$5-body problem. By identifying invariant subspaces and employing factorizations for characteristic polynomials, Moeckel further streamlined the analysis, emphasizing the crucial role of symmetry in this context.

Leandro systematically discussed the significance of symmetry in 2017, particularly focusing on ring systems. Leandro applied group representation theory and dihedral groups to exploit inherent symmetries, leading to a factorization of stability polynomials. Expanding on this methodology, Leandro applied these principles to investigate the structure and stability of the rhombus family of relative equilibria. These studies all revolve around computing eigenvalues for the Hessian, showcasing how symmetry aids in simplifying calculations.

In 2008, Xia introduced a novel method for studying symmetries within the Newtonian $$
M \ddot{r}=\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}
$$5-body problem. This approach was exemplified by determining eigenvalues for the Hessian of specific functions, showcasing how group representation and symmetry groups can simplify intricate problems. Expanding on Xia's work, we further refined this method in , applying it to streamline calculations for certain eigenvalue problems and elucidating the degenerate point $m^{*}$N$3507R^{2 n}$. From these computations, we identify the smallest subspaces that's simultaneously invariant under the actions of all elements of the symmetry group. It turns out that the dimension of each of these subspaces is no larger than 2. We then decompose the whole space as a direct sum of these invariant subspaces. In the end, matrices that are invariant under the dihedral group action can be simplified into block diagonal forms with the size of each block at most $M=\operatorname{diag}\left\{m_{1}, m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}, m_{N}\right\}$591. We further apply this method to analyze the Newtonian $$
M \ddot{r}=\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}
$$5-body problem and derive explicit formulas for eigenvalues of the corresponding Hessians. In Section 2 we establish the framework, while in Section 3 we will apply the framework to the regular $$
M \ddot{r}=\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}
$$5-gon central configuration in several situations.

For a comprehensive overview of group representation and central configurations in the Newtonian $$
M \ddot{r}=\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}
$$5-body problem, we refer interested readers to .

The method we presented in this paper is applicable to general cases where a linear function is invariant under a group action.

## 2006.13049v1

# Pfaffians and the inverse problem for collinear central configurations 

D.L. Ferrario<br>June 24, 2020


#### Abstract

We consider, after Albouy-Moeckel, the inverse problem for collinear central configurations: given a collinear configuration of $$
M \ddot{r}=\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}
$$5 bodies, find positive masses which make it central. We give some new estimates concerning the positivity of Albouy-Moeckel pfaffians: we show that for any homogeneity $$
M \ddot{r}=\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}
$$47 and $\mathbb{R}^{3}$061 or $n \left[\nabla f\left(\mathbf{x}^{(k)}\right)\right]2 10$ and $\pi / 3 \mathrm{rad}$573 (computerassisted) the pfaffians are positive. Moreover, for the inverse problem with positive masses, we show that for any homogeneity and $M=\operatorname{diag}\left\{m_{1}, m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}, m_{N}\right\}$047 there are explicit regions of the configuration space without solutions of the inverse problem.


Keywords: $$
M \ddot{r}=\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}
$$5-body problem; pfaffian; central configuration; inverse problem.
